entry: 1927 American part-talkie musical drama film directed by Alan Crosland. It was the first feature-length motion picture with synchronized recorded music and lip-synchronous singing and speech, in several isolated sequences. Its release, featuring six songs performed by Al Jolson on the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system, heralded the commercial ascendance of sound films and effectively ended the [[Silent film|silent film]] era. Adapted from Samson Raphaelson's 1925 play, it follows Jakie Rabinowitz, the son of a cantor who defies his devout family to become a [[Jazz|jazz]] singer performing in blackface. Darryl F. Zanuck won an Academy Honorary Award for producing it. The film's copyright expired on January 1, 2023, placing it in the [[Public domain|public domain]]. In 1996 it was selected for the United States National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]].

American rock band formed in [[Las Vegas]], Nevada, in 2001. Brandon Flowers and Dave Keuning were joined by Mark Stoermer and Ronnie Vannucci Jr. in 2002. The band's name comes from a fictional group in the [[Music video|music video]] for the [[New Order (band)|New Order]] song "Crystal." Each of its seven studio albums, beginning with *Hot Fuss* (2004), topped the UK Albums Chart. The Killers have sold more than 35 million records worldwide and headlined [[Wembley Stadium]] and [[Madison Square Garden]].

1895 short story collection by American writer Robert W. Chambers. Its first stories combine [[Supernatural|supernatural]] horror with weird fiction, centered on a forbidden play that induces madness in its readers. The collection gradually shifts toward romantic fiction, and several stories are set in [[Paris]]. Critics including E. F. Bleiler, S. T. Joshi, and T. E. D. Klein have described the horror stories as a classic in the field. Lin Carter called the book "an absolute masterpiece" of weird fantasy. It was an influence on H. P. Lovecraft.

English rock band formed in [[London]] in 1962. Its breakthrough, "You Really Got Me" (1964), topped the charts in the [[United Kingdom]]. Initially influenced by American [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]], the band later adopted British music hall and folk. Ray Davies's satirical songs about English life won acclaim on albums such as *The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society* (1968). The band had seventeen UK Top 20 singles and sold over 50 million records worldwide. Its original four members were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1990, and [[Blur (band)|Blur]] and [[Oasis (band)|Oasis]] cited it as a major influence.

Oil-on-canvas painting with added gold leaf by Austrian Symbolist painter [[Gustav Klimt]], painted 1907–08 at the height of what scholars call his "Golden Period." It depicts a couple embracing in robes decorated in a style influenced by [[Art Nouveau]] and the organic forms of the [[Arts and Crafts movement]]. Its gold leaf recalls medieval gold-ground paintings and earlier [[Mosaic|mosaics]]. It was exhibited in 1908 as *Liebespaar* (the lovers). The painting hangs in the Österreichische Galerie Belvedere in [[Vienna]] and is considered a masterpiece of the Vienna Secession and probably Klimt's most important work.

1899 [[Short story|short story]] by [[Anton Chekhov]]. It describes an adulterous affair between Dmitri Gurov, an unhappily married [[Moscow]] banker, and Anna Sergeyevna, a young married woman, which begins while both are vacationing alone in Yalta. After parting, Gurov unexpectedly falls in love with her and pursues her despite the obvious complications. [[Vladimir Nabokov]] considered it one of the greatest short stories ever written.

[[Mural]] painting by the Italian High Renaissance artist [[Leonardo da Vinci]], dated to c. 1495–1498, in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in [[Milan]]. It depicts the moment after [[Jesus]] announces that one of his twelve apostles will betray him, as told in the Gospel of John. Its handling of space, perspective, motion and emotion has made it one of the most recognizable paintings in the Western world. Leonardo used tempera on gesso, pitch and mastic, which allowed frequent revisions but contributed to its decay. Environmental factors and intentional damage have left little of the original, despite restoration attempts, the last completed in 1999. It is Leonardo's largest work apart from the Sala delle Asse.

2013 action-adventure game developed by Naughty Dog and published by Sony Computer Entertainment. Players control Joel, a smuggler escorting a teenage girl, Ellie, across a post-apocalyptic United States, and fight hostile humans and creatures infected by a mutated [[Fungus|fungus]]. Released for the [[PlayStation 3]], it sold over 1.3 million copies in its first week and 17 million by April 2018. It won several Game of the Year awards. A remastered [[PlayStation 4]] version followed in 2014, and the sequel, *The Last of Us Part II*, in 2020. An [[HBO]] television adaptation appeared in 2023.

1820 short story by American author Washington Irving, collected in *The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.* Irving wrote it while living in [[Birmingham]], [[England]]. Set in a valley near Tarrytown, it follows the superstitious schoolteacher Ichabod Crane, whose rival Brom Bones mocks and frightens him. Riding home after a party, Ichabod is pursued by the Headless Horseman, believed to be the ghost of a Hessian cavalryman who lost his head during the [[American Revolutionary War]]. The story has remained in print since its publication. A 1949 [[Walt Disney]] animation formed one segment of *The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad*.

headword: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
sort_key: legend of zelda breath of the wild
entry: 2017 action-adventure game developed by [[Nintendo]] Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) for the Wii U and [[Nintendo Switch]]. Players explore the open-world kingdom of Hyrule as Link, who sets out to save Princess Zelda and prevent Calamity Ganon from destroying the world. Its nonlinear design, physics-based "chemistry engine" and emphasis on experimentation made it a landmark of open-world design. Released March 3, 2017, it won the Game of the Year award at the 2017 Game Awards. It sold 35.76 million copies by June 2026, making it the bestselling [[The Legend of Zelda|Zelda]] game. A sequel, *The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom*, followed in 2023.

headword: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
sort_key: legend of zelda ocarina of time
entry: 1998 action-adventure game developed and published by [[Nintendo]] for the [[Nintendo 64]]. It was the first game in [[The Legend of Zelda|the series]] with 3D graphics, and it introduced a target-lock system and context-sensitive buttons that became common in 3D adventure games. The player, as Link, travels through time to stop the Gerudo king Ganondorf and must play songs on an [[Ocarina|ocarina]]. Critics praised its visuals, sound, gameplay and writing, and it is the highest-rated game on the review aggregators Metacritic and GameRankings. It sold more than seven million copies worldwide. A remake for the [[Nintendo 3DS]] appeared in 2011.

Video game series created by Japanese designers [[Shigeru Miyamoto]] and Takashi Tezuka. It is developed and published primarily by [[Nintendo]]. The series centers on incarnations of Link, a courageous boy of the elf-like Hylian race, and Princess Zelda, who fight to save the land of Hyrule from Ganon, an evil warlord turned demon king. Since the first game, [[The Legend of Zelda (video game)|The Legend of Zelda]], appeared in 1986, the series has grown to 21 entries on Nintendo's major consoles, along with spin-offs, an American animated television series aired in 1989, and manga. Gameplay mixes puzzles, action-adventure and exploration, with staples such as bombs, [[Boomerang|boomerangs]], keys and shields. The series has sold over 150 million copies as of September 2024.

1986 action-adventure game developed and published by [[Nintendo]] for the Family Computer Disk System. It is the first game in the series. Players control Link from a top-down perspective as he collects the eight fragments of the Triforce of Wisdom to rescue Princess Zelda from Ganon. Designed by [[Shigeru Miyamoto]] and Takashi Tezuka, it was developed alongside [[Super Mario Bros.]], released September 13, 1985. The game sold over 6.5 million copies. Its release on the [[Nintendo Entertainment System]] in North America in late 1987 was one of the first to include an internal battery for saving data.

1994 American [[Animation|animated]] musical drama film directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff. Produced by Walt Disney Feature Animation, it follows the lion prince Simba, whose uncle Scar murders his father, King Mufasa, and usurps the throne. Its plot draws on [[Hamlet]] and the [[Bible]]. Released June 24, 1994, it was praised for its music, story and animation. With an initial worldwide gross of $763 million, it was the highest-grossing film of 1994, and it remains the highest-grossing traditionally animated film. It won two [[Academy Awards]]. In 2016 it was selected for the United States National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]].

1943 novella written and illustrated by French writer and aviator Antoine de Saint-Exupéry. It was first published in English and French in the United States in April 1943, and in France after the liberation, since Saint-Exupéry's works had been banned by the Vichy Regime. A pilot whose plane crashes in the [[Sahara]] meets a young prince from a tiny [[Asteroid|asteroid]], B-612, who visits Earth and addresses themes of [[Loneliness|loneliness]], [[Friendship|friendship]] and [[Love|love]]. It became Saint-Exupéry's most successful work, with an estimated 200 million copies sold. By November 2024 it had been translated into 600 languages and dialects, second only to the [[Bible]] among the most translated works.

Epic high fantasy [[Novel|novel]] by English author [[J. R. R. Tolkien]], published in three volumes from 1954 to 1955. Set in Middle-earth, it began as a sequel to [[The Hobbit]] and was written in stages between 1937 and 1949. Its title refers to the Dark Lord Sauron, who created the One Ring. The story follows the hobbit Frodo Baggins and the Company of the Ring, including the wizard [[Gandalf]], on a quest to destroy the Ring in the fires of Mount Doom. Tolkien drew on philology, mythology, Christianity and his experiences in the [[World War I|First World War]]. One of the best-selling books ever written, it has sold over 150 million copies and was named Britain's best-loved novel in a 2003 poll by the [[BBC]]. It was adapted as a [[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|film trilogy]] by [[Peter Jackson]].

sort_key: lord of the rings film series
entry: 2001–2003 trilogy of fantasy films directed by [[Peter Jackson]], based on the novel by [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]. The films were shot simultaneously in [[New Zealand]] from 1999 to 2000, at a budget of $281 million. Among the highest-grossing film series of all time, they have grossed over $2.9 billion worldwide. The series won 17 [[Academy Awards]] from 30 nominations, including Best Picture for *The Return of the King*. In 2021 the [[Library of Congress]] selected *The Fellowship of the Ring* for preservation in the United States National Film Registry.

1791 [[Opera|opera]] by [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], in two acts with a German libretto by Emanuel Schikaneder. It is a Singspiel, mixing singing with spoken dialogue. It premiered on September 30, 1791, at the Freihaus-Theater in Vienna, two months before Mozart's death, and was his last opera. The Queen of the Night asks Prince Tamino to rescue her daughter Pamina from the high priest Sarastro. Instead, Tamino seeks to join Sarastro's community and undergoes trials of initiation, as does Pamina. The earthy Papageno fails the trials but is rewarded with Papagena. It was an outstanding success from its first performances and remains a staple of the repertory. Many scholars acknowledge an influence of [[Freemasonry]].

American folk rock vocal group formed in New York City in 1965. Led by songwriter John Phillips, whose harmonies adapted [[Folk music|folk]] to a new beat style, the group released five studio albums and 17 singles, six of which made the Billboard top 10. Its name was inspired by the [[Hells Angels]], whose female associates were called "mamas." The group broke up in 1968 and sold close to 40 million records worldwide. It reunited briefly to record *People Like Us* in 1971. The group was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1998.

1786 [[Opera|opera buffa]] in four acts by [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], with an Italian libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. Adapted from Beaumarchais's 1784 comedy, it tells how the servants Figaro and Susanna marry, foiling the efforts of their employer, Count Almaviva, to seduce Susanna. Emperor [[Joseph II]] initially banned Beaumarchais's play in Vienna, but Da Ponte obtained approval for an operatic version. It premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna on May 1, 1786. Set near [[Seville]], the opera recounts a single "day of madness." In a 2017 BBC News Magazine poll of 172 opera singers, it ranked first among 20 operas.

Satirical novel by Russian writer [[Mikhail Bulgakov]], written in the [[Soviet Union]] from 1928 to 1940. The devil, appearing as Professor Woland, visits atheist [[Moscow]] and challenges Soviet citizens' beliefs while condemning their behavior. A second strand follows the Master, a novelist whose manuscript about [[Pontius Pilate]] is denounced and destroyed. The novel satirizes Soviet bureaucracy and atheism, combining supernatural elements with Christian philosophy. A censored version appeared in the magazine *Moskva* in 1966–67. Bulgakov burned the first manuscript in 1930. The first book edition was published in [[Paris]] in 1967. Critics widely regard it as one of the greatest novels of the 20th century.

1999 science fiction–action film written and directed by [[The Wachowskis|the Wachowskis]]. It stars [[Keanu Reeves]] as Neo, a computer hacker who discovers that his life is an illusion created by intelligent machines. Released March 31, 1999, it grossed over $460 million on a $63 million budget. It won all four [[Academy Awards]] for which it was nominated, including Best Visual Effects. The film popularized "bullet time," a slow-motion effect in which the camera appears to move through the scene at normal speed. Two sequels were released in 2003, and a fourth film, *The Matrix Resurrections*, appeared in 2021.

1915 novella by [[Franz Kafka]]. It follows Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman who wakes to find himself transformed into a huge insect and struggles to adjust, as do his family. Confined to bed, he reflects on his job while his family loses its financial stability. In popular adaptations the insect is commonly depicted as a [[Cockroach|cockroach]]. Critics have offered varied interpretations. At about 70 printed pages, it is the longest of the stories Kafka considered complete and published during his lifetime. It first appeared in October 1915 in the journal *Die weißen Blätter*, and in book form in December 1915 in the series *Der jüngste Tag*.

American pop rock band formed in [[Los Angeles]] in the mid-1960s. The group was conceived in 1965 by television producers Bob Rafelson and Bert Schneider for an [[NBC]] [[Sitcom|sitcom]] of the same name. Session musicians such as the Wrecking Crew played on early recordings. From 1966 to 1967 the band had four consecutive number-one albums and three number-one singles, including "I'm a Believer." After gaining control of their recordings, the members broke up in the early 1970s. Interest in the television show revived in 1986, leading to reunions until 2011. Micky Dolenz became the sole surviving member after Michael Nesmith's death in 2021.

Goddess in Irish mythology associated with [[War|war]] and fate. Her name is often translated as "phantom queen" or "great queen." She foretells doom, death or victory in battle and often appears as a crow, the badb. She incites warriors and is portrayed washing the bloodstained clothes of those fated to die. She is usually described as one of three sisters, the "three Morrígna," with Badb and Macha. She is associated with the later [[Banshee|banshee]] of folklore, and some modern writers have linked her to [[Morgan le Fay]].
